intro: This guide takes your group through “The Practice of the Presence of God (For Teens)” in thirteen weeks, one chapter a week. It tells the story of Nicolas Herman, a clumsy former soldier and footman who became Brother Lawrence, the cook in a Paris monastery, and draws on his conversations and letters to show how anyone can live with God through an ordinary day. It is written for teens aged about 13 to 18 and suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or beforehand at home (6–8 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own (2–3 minutes). Each chapter also ends with a practical step for the week; it’s worth asking at the start of the next session how it went.

To prepare, read the chapter and try its weekly practice yourself, so you can speak from experience. Two chapters need particular care. Chapter 4 describes years in which Lawrence was tormented by the fear that he was damned; some teens carry fears like that, or anxious and intrusive thoughts more generally, so take them seriously, follow the chapter’s own advice that no one should suffer alone, and be ready to involve parents, a pastor or professional help. Chapter 12 is about serious illness and Lawrence’s death, and may touch anyone who is ill or has lost someone; be gentle, and underline the chapter’s point that taking medicine and seeing a doctor go hand in hand with trusting God.

weeks.summary: Nicolas Herman was born around 1614 in Lorraine, was wounded as a soldier, and became a footman who called himself “a great awkward fellow who broke everything.” He later became Brother Lawrence, a lay brother in a Paris monastery, and a priest named Joseph de Beaufort wrote down their conversations from 1666 because people said this ordinary man lived close to God. The chapter introduces his lifelong habit: remembering that God is with you and talking to him all day long. The big idea: God isn’t waiting for us to become impressive; he looks at the heart.

memory_verse.text: For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.

activity.title: Outward or Heart?
steps: Ask the group to list the things people their age are usually judged on, and write them down.
Next to each, discuss whether it is “outward appearance” or “heart.”
Read aloud Nicolas’s description of himself and ask why God might choose someone like that.
Ask everyone to write privately the three things they feel worst at, then to pray over the list on their own this week as the chapter suggests.

weeks.summary: At eighteen, Nicolas looked at a bare tree in winter and realised that leaves, flowers and fruit would come back without anyone gluing them on. Through that ordinary moment he received a view of God’s providence and power that, more than forty years later, had never been rubbed out, and it set him loose from the world. The chapter says the whole world preaches about God’s care, and the question is whether we slow down to notice. The big idea: practising God’s presence begins with paying attention.

memory_verse.text: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork.

activity.title: Ten Minutes of Looking
activity.materials: Nothing (or a window or a short walk outside)
steps: Ask everyone to put their phones away for the activity.
Go outside, or to a window, and give each person two or three silent minutes to look properly at one ordinary thing.
Come back together and let each person say what they looked at and one thing it showed them about God.
Talk about what usually stops us from noticing, and agree on one way to slow down this week.

weeks.summary: In 1640 Nicolas joined the Discalced Carmelites in Paris as a lay brother and took the name Brother Lawrence. He went in expecting to be made to smart for his awkwardness and faults, but, as Beaufort wrote, “God had disappointed him”: he found nothing but satisfaction, and later spoke of “perfect liberty and continual joy.” The chapter challenges the suspicion that following God properly makes life smaller and sadder. The big idea: closeness to God is not a punishment to put up with; it is the joy our hearts were made for.

memory_verse.text: You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.

activity.title: Smaller or Fuller?
activity.materials: A whiteboard or large sheet of paper
steps: Draw two columns: “What people think following God takes away” and “What following God actually gives.”
Let the group fill the first column honestly.
Then fill the second column together, using the chapter and the memory verse.
Ask everyone to think privately of one thing they are afraid they would have to give up, and to tell God about it in a silent prayer.

weeks.summary: For years Brother Lawrence was convinced he would be damned, and he wrote that for the first ten years he suffered much and felt that everything was against him. He resolved that, whatever became of him, he would keep acting purely for the love of God, and in time he saw that his fear came from a lack of faith, found himself “changed all at once,” and felt a profound inward peace. The chapter urges readers not to suffer alone as he did, but to tell someone they trust. The big idea: holding on to God while the feelings are still bad is real faith, and his love casts out fear.

memory_verse.text: There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.

activity.title: Who Can I Tell?
steps: Read Lawrence’s resolution aloud: “whatever becomes of me… I will always continue to act purely for the love of God.”
Talk together about the difference between feelings and the truth about God, using the chapter.
Point out that Lawrence “consulted nobody,” and ask why people keep fears to themselves.
Ask each person to write privately, on a card to keep, the names of two people they could talk to if a fear about God, or any fear, kept coming back.
Let the group know that you are one of those people, and when they can find you.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence read many books full of methods and stages and found they puzzled him more than they helped. He resolved to “give the all for the all” and began to live “as if there was none but He and I in the world,” turning his mind back to God whenever it wandered, at prayer times and all day long. It was hard at first, but the repeated acts became a habit. The big idea: methods can help, but the one thing needed is God himself.

memory_verse.text: Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary.

activity.title: Strip It Back
steps: Ask the group to list every Christian habit, app, plan or method they have heard of or tried.
Discuss which have genuinely helped and which became one more thing to feel behind on.
Read Lawrence’s line “as if there was none but He and I in the world” and ask what it means in a busy life.
Have each person write down one short prayer they could say anywhere, and agree to use only that all week.

weeks.summary: The monastery needed a cook, so Brother Lawrence cooked for about fifteen years, though he had a strong dislike of the work. He prayed before starting, talked to God as he worked, offered each task to him, and looked back honestly afterwards, giving thanks or asking forgiveness. People noticed his calm in the busiest moments, and he said he possessed God in the clatter of the kitchen as much as on his knees. The big idea: we don’t have to escape the noise to be with God; work done with him is never wasted.

memory_verse.text: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.

activity.title: My Kitchen
steps: Ask each person to write down the task in their week they like least: a subject, a chore, a job.
Read Lawrence’s kitchen prayer aloud, then have everyone rewrite it in their own words for their own task.
In pairs, compare the prayers and talk about how doing the task “with God” might change it.
Agree to pray the prayer before that task this week, and to report back next session.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence was glad to pick up a straw from the ground for the love of God, because God “regards not the greatness of the work, but the love with which it is performed.” He taught that holiness does not depend on changing our works but on doing for God’s sake what we normally do for ourselves. Later moved to mending sandals, he was content anywhere, and warned against growing weary of little things done for God. The big idea: small jobs done with great love are where faithfulness is learned.

memory_verse.text: One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.

activity.title: Secret Straws
steps: Ask the group to brainstorm small, unnoticed jobs they could do at home, at school or at church.
Talk about why it is harder to be faithful when nobody is watching.
Have each person write privately one small job a day they will do for someone else, for God, this week.
Agree not to tell anyone what they did, only to tell God at the end of the week.

weeks.summary: The monastery twice sent Brother Lawrence to buy its wine, a task he found very unwelcome, and on the boat to Burgundy his leg was so bad he had to roll over the barrels. He told God it was his business he was about, and found it all very well done. His habit was to say, “Lord, I cannot do this unless Thou enablest me,” and he received strength more than sufficient. The big idea: planning is doing what we can, but worrying is trying to carry what only God can.

memory_verse.text: Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.

activity.title: Plan or Worry?
steps: Have each person write privately one thing coming up that they are dreading.
Under it, ask them to draw two columns: “What I can do to prepare” and “What only God can carry.”
Let them fill in both columns, then invite anyone who wishes to share one practical step.
Pray Lawrence’s prayer together: “Lord, I can’t do this unless you help me.”

weeks.summary: Someone wrote to Brother Lawrence about wandering thoughts in prayer, and he replied that this was nothing new; he had spent whole prayer times rejecting distractions and falling back into them. He advised keeping prayer simple, like a beggar waiting at a rich man’s gate, bringing the mind back calmly instead of getting upset, and turning to God often during the day so prayer becomes a continued conversation. The big idea: everyone’s mind wanders; the turning back is itself the prayer, and God is glad each time we return.

memory_verse.text: You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.

activity.title: Back to You
steps: Explain that the group will spend three minutes in silent prayer together.
Ask everyone to say silently “back to you, Lord” each time they notice their mind has wandered, and to keep a private count.
Afterwards, ask how it went, without anyone needing to give their number.
Read Lawrence’s advice about not getting troubled, and ask how calm returning differs from scolding yourself.

weeks.summary: When Brother Lawrence failed, he confessed it plainly, told God he would never do otherwise if left to himself, and then gave himself no further uneasiness about it. He was aware of his faults but not discouraged by them, expected pardon through the blood of Jesus Christ, and came back after times of forgetting God with even greater trust. He said that by rising after his falls he came to find it hard not to think of God. The big idea: the goal is not a perfect record but a quick return.

memory_verse.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

activity.title: Excuse, Spiral or Return
steps: Describe three responses to failure: making excuses, spiralling into guilt, and Lawrence’s quick return.
Read out some everyday situations, such as losing your temper, lying to a parent, ignoring God for a month, and ask what each response would look like.
Talk about why the quick return is not the same as taking sin lightly.
Remind the group that if they hurt someone, the return includes putting it right with that person too.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence wrote about a young soldier with a good heart but “a great deal of youth,” who had no time for long prayers. His answer was that “a little lifting up of the heart suffices,” even on the march with a sword in hand, and that nobody will notice these quick prayers. He told friends to make “an oratory of our heart” and not to leave God alone, as it would be rude to leave a visiting friend. The big idea: praying without ceasing means a friendship with God that never really goes quiet.

activity.title: Everyday Triggers
steps: Ask the group to list the moments in a normal school day when nobody would notice a two-second prayer.
Have each person choose three triggers, such as a doorway, a meal or picking up a phone.
Ask them to write a short prayer for each trigger: “Thank you,” “Help me” or “I’m here.”
Agree to try the triggers all week and compare notes next session.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence’s last letters were to a seriously ill friend. Old and in pain himself, he prayed not only for relief but for strength and patience to bear it, believing God is often nearer in sickness than in health, and admitting that God sometimes hides himself. The chapter adds that his advice about medicines belongs to the 1600s, and that taking medicine and trusting God go together. Lawrence died in February 1691, a week after taking to his bed. The big idea: in suffering we can ask God for strength to go through it with him, not only to make it stop.

memory_verse.text: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.

activity.title: Pray Both Ways
steps: Ask each person to think of one person they know who is ill or suffering, without naming them aloud unless they want to.
Have them write a short prayer for that person in two parts: one for relief, and one for strength and God’s closeness.
Talk together about why Lawrence prayed the second kind, and why it is still right to pray the first.
Encourage each person to send that person a short message this week to say they are thinking of them.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence admitted he was always saying the same thing: think of God often, talk to him and trust him, because it was the best and easiest method he knew. He said it needs no art or science, only a heart set on God, and that the habit is built one small repetition at a time, warning that one does not become holy all at once. He ends with an invitation: “Let us begin, then… Have courage.” The big idea: you can begin today, in the middle of an ordinary life, with one generous resolution.

memory_verse.text: Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.

activity.title: One Generous Resolution
steps: Ask the group to recall the habits from the book, such as the kitchen prayer, the straw from the ground and the everyday triggers, and list them.
Have each person pick the one habit they most want to keep.
Ask everyone to write themselves a short resolution beginning “God, I want to be with you today,” with the time of day they will say it.
Close by reading Lawrence’s chain of questions aloud and praying for one another to begin.
